nameStory: The "pincushion" name comes from this moss's distinctive growth habit of forming tight, rounded cushions that look remarkably like old-fashioned sewing pincushions. When you spot these compact, dome-shaped clusters growing on rocks, it's easy to imagine sticking pins right into their dense, bristly surface. The scientific name "cirrata" means "curled," referring to the way the leaves curl and twist when dry.
description: Common Pincushion is a small moss that forms distinctive rounded cushions or mounds on rocks and tree bark. These compact clumps typically measure just 1-2 inches across and rise about half an inch high, creating perfect little domes of green. Each cushion is made up of hundreds of tiny individual moss plants growing so closely together they appear as one solid mass. The overall effect is remarkably neat and geometric, like nature's own perfectly sculpted pillows.

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Forms tight, rounded cushions that feel firm and springy when gently pressed, like a dense sponge or small pillow

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Tiny narrow leaves that curl and twist dramatically when dry, giving the cushion a fuzzy, almost woolly appearance

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Dense and compact when moist, becoming more bristly and rough-textured as it dries out

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Bright green when wet, turning yellowish-green to brownish when dry, with the color change happening remarkably quickly

idTips.label: Sporophytes
idTips.description: Produces small reddish-brown capsules on thin stalks that emerge from the cushion centers, resembling tiny lollipops

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Almost exclusively found on exposed rock surfaces, particularly granite and other acidic rocks in sunny or partially shaded locations

habitat: Look for Common Pincushion on exposed rock faces, boulders, and stone walls throughout New England's forests and mountainous areas. It particularly favors acidic rocks like granite and prefers spots that receive some direct sunlight but aren't completely exposed all day. You'll often find it growing alongside other rock-dwelling mosses on cliff faces, rocky outcrops, and the stone foundations of old buildings.

seasonality.spring: Cushions turn their brightest green as moisture returns, and sporophytes begin developing their characteristic reddish stalks. This is the best time to see the dramatic color contrast between the green cushions and red-brown capsules.
seasonality.summer: Sporophytes mature and release spores, while the cushions may appear more yellowish during dry spells but quickly green up after rain showers.
seasonality.fall: Cushions remain visible but may take on brownish tones during extended dry periods. The compact growth form becomes more apparent as surrounding vegetation dies back.
seasonality.winter: Still visible under snow, the cushions maintain their shape and can be found year-round, though they appear most brown and dormant during the coldest months.

funFact: This tiny moss can survive being completely dried out for months, appearing dead and crunchy, but will turn bright green and start photosynthesizing again within minutes of getting wet—faster than you can make a cup of coffee!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other cushion-forming mosses, but Common Pincushion's cushions are notably more perfectly rounded and compact than most others. Remember: if it looks like you could use it as a tiny ottoman, and it's growing on rock, you've probably found your pincushion moss.
compareHints: Since Common Pincushion is the only Dicranoweisia species commonly found in New England, compare it with other cushion-forming rock mosses in the broader Dicranales order. Unlike many of its relatives that form looser tufts or mats, Common Pincushion creates much more densely packed, geometrically perfect cushions. Its leaves also curl more dramatically when dry compared to similar species, giving it a distinctly shaggy appearance during drought conditions.
